2.definition: The Russian name for the roughly two-and-a-half centuries (1240–1480) during which the Russian principalities were tribute-paying subjects of the Mongol Golden Horde. The word "yoke" comes from the heavy wooden harness laid across the necks of oxen; how oppressive the overlordship actually was, day to day, is a genuine historical debate.

4.definition: A shorthand for the mixed character of the Golden Horde and its successor khanates, whose ruling elite descended from Genghis Khan's Mongols but who increasingly spoke Turkic languages and absorbed Turkic and Islamic culture over the generations after the conquest.

Deliberately destroying a rival's eyes — a recognized form of medieval political mutilation used across the Orthodox world and Byzantium. A blinded man was held unfit to rule or lead armies but did not have to be killed, so it served as a substitute for execution that avoided the sin and blood-feud of murdering a kinsman.

6.definition: The river south of Moscow where, in 1480, Ivan III's army and the Great Horde faced each other across the water for weeks until the Horde withdrew — the bloodless 'Great Stand' that ended Mongol overlordship.

11.definition: Of the military and administrative methods then spreading from western and central Europe — here, infantry and cavalry drilled in volley fire and pike-and-musket tactics, organized and equipped on the model of contemporary European armies rather than older Muscovite levies.

12.definition: A Russian boyar (high-noble) family that rose to prominence as in-laws of Tsar Alexis through his first wife, Maria Miloslavskaya. After Alexis remarried into the rival Naryshkin family, the two clans became bitter competitors for influence over the succession.
